title: Jeremiah
summary: Jeremiah is a biblical book focused on prophetic calling, covenant breach, judgment, exile, new covenant, and restoration.
historical_context: Jeremiah interprets Judah's collapse and exile while announcing new covenant hope.
ancient_near_east_context: Jeremiah belongs to the ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern world reflected in its setting, institutions, and canonical placement.
hebraic_worldview: Jeremiah should be read with attention to covenant memory, communal identity, worship, wisdom, and accountability before the Lord.
second_temple_context: Second Temple readers received Jeremiah as part of Israel's Scriptures and read it within questions of identity, worship, exile, and hope.
canonical_context: Within Major Prophets, book 2 of 5, Jeremiah contributes to the Bible's unfolding witness by connecting prophetic calling, covenant breach, judgment, exile, new covenant, and restoration to the larger storyline.
later_christian_reception: Christian interpretation has read Jeremiah as part of the canonical witness to faithfulness, judgment, mercy, and hope in Christ-centered Scripture reading.
literary_context: Jeremiah uses prophecy, poetry within Major Prophets, book 2 of 5 to develop its themes through the book's structure and key passages.
covenantal_significance: Jeremiah helps readers trace covenant faithfulness, failure, mercy, and hope within its canonical setting.
authorship_positions: Traditional prophetic attribution to the named prophet
Many scholars note later collection and occasional expansion
date_ranges: 8th-6th centuries BCE with later shaping in some books
Final forms often reflect exilic or post-exilic editing
original_audience: Judah and Israel in crisis, facing judgment, exile, and restoration hopes
historical_setting: The late monarchic, exilic, and post-exilic periods
canonical_role: Jeremiah anchors prophetic calling, covenant breach, judgment, exile, new covenant, and restoration within Major Prophets, book 2 of 5 and connects the book to related people, places, events, and themes.
interpretive_disputes: How judgment and hope are balanced

related_objects.notes: Jeremiah is the prophetic figure associated with the book.
Jerusalem's fall is central to the book's crisis.
Babylonian exile frames much of the book.
The new covenant promise is a major canonical anchor.
Judgment is paired with promised restoration.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Jeremiah first within its own literary setting before moving to broader canonical connections.
The relationship links on Jeremiah are orientation anchors, not a full interpretive outline of the book.
